questions.q: Which vein in the cubital fossa is the first-choice site for routine adult venepuncture because it is large, well-anchored, and distant from major nerves and arteries?
options: Median cubital vein
Basilic vein
Accessory cephalic vein
Brachial vein
questions.explain: The median cubital vein is superficial, well-supported by surrounding tissue so it does not roll easily, and separated from the underlying brachial artery and median nerve by the bicipital aponeurosis.

open.q: Which superficial vein in the cubital fossa is the preferred first-choice site for routine venepuncture?

questions.q: Why should blood samples for coagulation studies (PT, aPTT) be collected in a light-blue-top sodium citrate tube filled to its exact marked fill line?
options: Sodium citrate inhibits glycolysis to prevent false reductions in clotting factors
Underfilling alters the critical 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio and artificially prolongs clotting times
Sodium citrate permanently chelates calcium so clotting cannot be re-initiated in the laboratory
Excess citrate causes in vitro haemolysis and hyperkalaemia
questions.explain: Coagulation tubes require an exact 9:1 ratio of blood to 3.2% sodium citrate; underfilling leaves excess unbound citrate that binds the calcium added during laboratory testing, falsely prolonging PT and aPTT.

open.q: What laboratory error occurs if a light-blue sodium citrate coagulation tube is underfilled during venepuncture?
accept: Excess citrate binds added calcium and prolongs clotting times

questions.q: Which blood collection tube additive is required when sending a venous sample for fasting plasma glucose estimation to prevent red blood cell glycolysis?
options: EDTA (lavender top)
Lithium heparin (green top)
Sodium fluoride with potassium oxalate (grey top)
Plain clot activator (red top)
questions.explain: Sodium fluoride inhibits the glycolytic enzyme enolase in erythrocytes, preventing glucose consumption in vitro while potassium oxalate acts as an anticoagulant.

open.q: Which chemical additive in a grey-top blood tube inhibits erythrocyte glycolysis for accurate plasma glucose measurement?

questions.q: During blood draw order, why must a lavender-top EDTA tube never be filled before a light-blue sodium citrate tube or serum electrolyte tube?
options: EDTA causes immediate clotting of the needle lumen
EDTA evaporates rapidly if exposed to air first
EDTA dilutes plasma proteins by 50%
Carryover of potassium-EDTA contaminates subsequent tubes, causing spurious hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, and prolonged clotting times
questions.explain: EDTA is a potent calcium chelator usually formulated as a potassium salt; cross-contamination falsely elevates serum potassium and lowers calcium and magnesium while prolonging coagulation assays.

open.q: What electrolyte and coagulation artefacts result if potassium-EDTA contaminates a chemistry or coagulation sample?
accept: Falsely elevated potassium, falsely low calcium, and prolonged clotting times

questions.q: Which bedside test must be performed before radial artery puncture for arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling to verify adequate collateral ulnar arterial perfusion to the hand?
options: Modified Allen's test
Trendelenburg test
Phalen's test
Buerger's test
questions.explain: The modified Allen's test assesses patency of the ulnar artery and palmar arch collateral circulation so the hand remains perfused if radial artery thrombosis or spasm occurs.

open.q: Name the bedside clinical test performed prior to radial artery cannulation or ABG puncture to confirm collateral ulnar blood supply.

questions.q: What are the normal adult reference ranges for arterial pH and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) on an arterial blood gas?
questions.explain: Normal arterial blood pH is tightly maintained between 7.35 and 7.45, with normal PaCO2 between 35 and 45 mmHg (4.7-6.0 kPa) and bicarbonate between 22 and 26 mmol/L.

open.q: State the normal adult reference range for arterial pH and PaCO2 in mmHg.
accept: pH 7.35 to 7.45 and PaCO2 35 to 45 mmHg

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman with severe diabetic ketoacidosis has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.18, PaCO2 22 mmHg, and HCO3- 9 mmol/L. Which acid-base disturbance is present?
options: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
Primary metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
questions.explain: Low pH (<7.35) with markedly reduced HCO3- (<22 mmol/L) indicates primary metabolic acidosis, while the low PaCO2 (<35 mmHg) reflects compensatory Kussmaul hyperventilation that has not yet normalized the pH.

open.q: Interpret an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.18, PaCO2 22 mmHg, and bicarbonate 9 mmol/L.

questions.q: At which vertebral interspace is a diagnostic lumbar puncture safely performed in an adult to avoid injuring the spinal cord?
options: T12-L1 or L1-L2 interspace
C7-T1 interspace
S2-S3 sacral hiatus
L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace (aligned with Tuffier's intercristal line)
questions.explain: Because the adult conus medullaris terminates at the lower border of L1 (or upper L2), inserting the spinal needle at L3-L4 or L4-L5 enters the lumbar cistern containing only mobile cauda equina nerve roots.

open.q: At which vertebral interspaces is a lumbar puncture performed in adults, and what anatomical landmark guides this level?
accept: L3-L4 or L4-L5 guided by the intercristal (Tuffier's) line
L3-L4 or L4-L5 along the iliac crests

questions.q: Which clinical finding is an absolute contraindication to performing an immediate lumbar puncture without prior cranial neuroimaging due to the risk of fatal cerebral herniation?
options: Papilloedema and focal lateralizing neurological deficits suggesting raised intracranial pressure with mass effect
High fever of 39.5 degrees Celsius with nuchal rigidity
Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT brain scan
Positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs without focal signs
questions.explain: Removing CSF from below when an intracranial space-occupying lesion causes raised intracranial pressure creates a pressure gradient that can precipitate downward uncal or cerebellar tonsillar herniation.

open.q: Why are papilloedema and focal neurological deficits strict contraindications to immediate lumbar puncture before neuroimaging?
accept: Risk of cerebral herniation due to raised intracranial pressure
Can precipitate brain herniation or coning
Raised ICP with mass effect risks herniation

questions.q: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis from a febrile young adult shows a cloudy appearance, opening pressure of 32 cmH2O, polymorphonuclear neutrophil predominance (>1000 cells/microL), markedly elevated protein, and CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of 0.2. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Viral (aseptic) meningitis
Acute bacterial meningitis
Multiple sclerosis
Guillain-Barre syndrome
questions.explain: Bacterial meningitis classically produces turbid CSF with high opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and marked hypoglycorrhachia (CSF glucose <40% of simultaneous blood glucose).

open.q: Which central nervous system infection produces turbid CSF with neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and markedly reduced CSF-to-serum glucose ratio?

questions.q: Where should the needle be inserted during diagnostic thoracentesis to avoid injuring the intercostal neurovascular bundle?
options: Along the inferior border of the upper rib
Directly through the mid-body of the rib
Just superior to the upper border of the lower rib in the intercostal space
Through the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
questions.explain: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove along the inferior margin of each rib; advancing the needle over the superior margin of the lower rib safely avoids them.

open.q: Along which margin of a rib should a thoracentesis needle be advanced to avoid damaging the intercostal neurovascular bundle?
accept: Superior border of the lower rib
Upper margin of the lower rib
Top edge of the rib below

questions.q: According to Light's criteria, which biochemical finding classifies a pleural effusion as an exudate rather than a transudate?
options: Pleural fluid protein-to-serum protein ratio less than 0.3
Pleural fluid LDH-to-serum LDH ratio less than 0.4
Pleural fluid glucose equal to simultaneous serum glucose
Pleural fluid protein-to-serum protein ratio greater than 0.5
questions.explain: Light's criteria define an exudative pleural effusion if at least one of the following is met: pleural-to-serum protein ratio >0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural LDH >two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

open.q: State the three biochemical thresholds that make up Light's criteria for an exudative pleural effusion.
accept: Pleural-to-serum protein ratio > 0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural LDH > two-thirds upper limit of normal serum LDH
Protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, pleural LDH > 2/3 ULN

questions.q: What is the standard anatomical needle entry site for diagnostic or therapeutic abdominal paracentesis in a patient with gross ascites?
options: Left lower quadrant, 2-3 cm medial and superior to the anterior superior iliac spine (lateral to the rectus sheath)
Right upper quadrant just below the costal margin
Midline 2 cm above the umbilicus through the falciform ligament
Directly over the inferior epigastric artery midpoint
questions.explain: The left lower quadrant (lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle, avoiding the inferior epigastric vessels and the caecum on the right) is the safest and thinnest abdominal wall site for paracentesis.

open.q: Which abdominal quadrant and anatomical landmark is preferred for safe needle insertion during abdominal paracentesis?
accept: Left lower quadrant lateral to the rectus sheath
Left iliac fossa medial and superior to the ASIS

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with ascites has a serum albumin of 36 g/L and ascitic fluid albumin of 18 g/L. What is his Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG), and what mechanism does it indicate?
options: SAAG = 18 g/L (1.8 g/dL), indicating peritoneal carcinomatosis without portal hypertension
SAAG = 18 g/L (1.8 g/dL), indicating portal hypertension
SAAG = 2.0 g/L (0.2 g/dL), indicating tuberculous peritonitis
SAAG = 54 g/L (5.4 g/dL), indicating nephrotic syndrome
questions.explain: SAAG equals serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin (36 - 18 = 18 g/L or 1.8 g/dL); a SAAG >= 11 g/L (1.1 g/dL) indicates portal hypertension with 97% accuracy.

open.q: What threshold value of the Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites?
accept: Greater than or equal to 11 g/L or 1.1 g/dL

questions.q: How should an adult male penis be positioned during insertion of a Foley urethral catheter to straighten the anterior urethra and ease passage?
options: Pressed flat downward against the scrotum
Rotated 90 degrees laterally
Held upright perpendicular (90 degrees) to the abdominal wall with gentle traction
Flexed downward toward the thighs
questions.explain: Holding the penis upright at 90 degrees to the body with gentle upward traction eliminates the natural penoscrotal curve of the anterior urethra, minimizing urethral trauma during catheter advancement.

open.q: In what direction should the penis be held during male urethral catheterization to straighten the anterior urethra?

questions.q: Which clinical finding is a strict contraindication to blind urethral catheterization in a trauma patient?
options: Suprapubic bladder dullness
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
Microscopic haematuria on dipstick
Blood at the external urethral meatus with a perineal haematoma or high-riding prostate
questions.explain: Blood at the urethral meatus, scrotal/perineal bruising, or a high-riding prostate signals potential urethral disruption; blind catheterization can convert a partial tear into a complete transection, so retrograde urethrography is required first.

open.q: What triad of trauma signs contraindicates blind urethral catheterization due to suspected urethral injury?
accept: Blood at the urethral meatus, perineal haematoma, and high-riding prostate
Meatal blood, perineal bruising, and high-riding prostate

questions.q: How is the external insertion length of a nasogastric (NG) tube estimated at the bedside before placement?
options: Measuring from the tip of the nose to the earlobe and down to the xiphoid process (NEX distance)
Measuring from the chin to the umbilicus
Measuring from the forehead to the sternal angle
Inserting a fixed 25 cm in all adult patients
questions.explain: The NEX measurement (Nose to Earlobe to Xiphisternum) estimates the distance from the nares through the oesophagus into the gastric fundus.

open.q: Which three anatomical landmarks are used to estimate the insertion length of a nasogastric tube?
accept: Tip of the nose, earlobe, and xiphoid process

questions.q: Which first-line bedside test confirms correct intragastric placement of a nasogastric tube before initiating enteral feeding?
options: Auscultating over the epigastrium while injecting 20 mL of air ('whoosh test')
Testing aspirated fluid with pH indicator paper showing pH <= 5.5
Submerging the external tube end in water to check for bubbling
Observing whether the patient can speak clearly
questions.explain: Aspirate pH <= 5.5 reliably confirms gastric acid environment; the air insufflation 'whoosh test' is unreliable because sounds from a tube in the bronchus or pleural space transmit to the epigastrium.

open.q: What first-line bedside test and threshold value confirm intragastric placement of a nasogastric tube?
accept: Gastric aspirate pH less than or equal to 5.5

questions.q: Where is precordial chest lead V4 placed during a standard 12-lead ECG recording?
options: Right 4th intercostal space at the sternal border
Left 4th intercostal space at the sternal border
Left 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
Left 5th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line
questions.explain: Lead V4 is positioned in the left 5th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line, serving as the anatomical anchor for V3 (midway between V2 and V4), V5 (anterior axillary line), and V6 (mid-axillary line).

open.q: State the exact anatomical placement for precordial ECG lead V4.
accept: Left 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
Left fifth intercostal space midclavicular line

questions.q: At the standard ECG paper speed of 25 mm/s, how much time does one large 5 mm square represent?
options: 0.04 seconds
0.10 seconds
0.50 seconds
0.20 seconds
questions.explain: At 25 mm/s, each small 1 mm square equals 0.04 seconds (40 ms), and one large 5 mm square equals 5 x 0.04 = 0.20 seconds (200 ms), so 300 large squares equal 1 minute.

open.q: At standard ECG paper speed of 25 mm/s, how many seconds are represented by one small square (1 mm) and one large square (5 mm)?
accept: 0.04 seconds for one small square and 0.20 seconds for one large square

questions.q: Why is an erect posteroanterior (PA) chest radiograph preferred over an anteroposterior (AP) film when evaluating cardiomegaly?
options: In a PA view, the anterior heart is closer to the X-ray detector, minimizing geometric magnification of the cardiac silhouette
AP films expose the patient to ten times more ionizing radiation
PA films eliminate the need for deep inspiration
AP films cannot visualize the costophrenic angles
questions.explain: Because the heart sits anteriorly in the thorax, a PA projection places it against the film cassette, avoiding the artificial beam-divergence magnification seen on AP films where cardiothoracic ratio cannot be reliably measured.

open.q: Why does an anteroposterior (AP) chest X-ray artificially enlarge the cardiac silhouette compared to a posteroanterior (PA) film?
accept: The anterior heart is farther from the detector causing geometric magnification
X-ray beam divergence magnifies the anterior heart
Geometric magnification due to greater heart-to-film distance

questions.q: What does a positive leukocyte esterase combined with positive nitrites on a urine dipstick test strongly suggest?
options: Uncontrolled diabetic ketoacidosis
Bacterial urinary tract infection (typically Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae)
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria
Primary nephrotic syndrome
questions.explain: Leukocyte esterase indicates pyuria (white blood cells in urine), while nitrites reflect bacterial conversion of urinary nitrates by Gram-negative organisms such as Escherichia coli.

open.q: What clinical condition is indicated by positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites on a urine dipstick?

questions.q: Which aseptic step is essential before inoculating venous blood into aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles to prevent false-positive skin contaminant growth?
options: Wiping the skin with dry cotton wool only
Inoculating the anaerobic bottle first using an air-filled syringe
Disinfecting both the patient's skin and the rubber septa of the culture bottles with 70% alcohol/chlorhexidine and allowing them to air dry completely
Placing the blood culture bottles inside an ice bucket immediately after collection
questions.explain: Allowing alcohol/chlorhexidine skin and bottle-top antisepsis to air dry ensures bactericidal contact time and prevents residual alcohol from killing fastidious pathogens in the bottle; blood cultures are kept at room temperature or incubated, never iced.

open.q: Why must alcohol or chlorhexidine skin antiseptic be allowed to air dry completely before performing venepuncture for blood cultures?
accept: To achieve full bactericidal effect and prevent alcohol from killing organisms in the culture bottle
Ensures adequate contact time for skin disinfection
Prevents skin flora contamination and bactericidal carryover

questions.q: Which anatomical site is most commonly used in adults for both bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy?
options: Manubrium of the sternum
Proximal tibial tuberosity
Greater trochanter of the femur
Posterior superior iliac spine (iliac crest)
questions.explain: The posterior superior iliac spine is safe, rich in active haematopoietic marrow in adults, distant from vital mediastinal organs (unlike the sternum), and permits both aspiration and core trephine biopsy.

open.q: Which anatomical site is the standard preferred location for bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy in adults?

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with severe pneumonia and cold, clammy fingers has a pulse oximeter reading of 84% despite looking comfortable and having normal arterial blood gas PaO2 of 92 mmHg. What is the most likely cause of this discrepancy?
options: Peripheral vasoconstriction and poor digital perfusion reducing pulsatile signal detection
Carbon monoxide poisoning artificially lowering SpO2
Severe polycythaemia causing true arterial desaturation
Hypoglycaemia altering haemoglobin light absorption
questions.explain: Pulse oximetry relies on pulsatile arterial blood flow in the fingertip; cold extremities, hypotension, or peripheral vasoconstriction impair signal detection and yield falsely low SpO2 readings despite normal arterial oxygenation.

open.q: Name two common clinical factors that cause a pulse oximeter to display a falsely low SpO2 reading despite normal arterial PaO2.
accept: Cold extremities and poor peripheral perfusion
Hypotension and poor digital blood flow
